title: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice
abstract: The psychological principles that govern the perception of decision problems and the evaluation of probabilities and outcomes produce predictable shifts of preference when the same problem is framed in different ways. Reversals of preference are demonstrated in choices regarding monetary outcomes, both hypothetical and real, and in questions pertaining to the loss of human lives. The effects of frames on preferences are compared to the effects of perspectives on perceptual appearance. The dependence of preferences on the formulation of decision problems is a significant concern for the theory of rational choice.

claims.text: Psychological principles governing decision problem perception and evaluation of probabilities and outcomes produce predictable shifts of preference when problems are framed differently.
Reversals of preference occur in choices regarding hypothetical monetary outcomes depending on framing.
Reversals of preference occur in choices regarding real monetary outcomes depending on framing.
Reversals of preference occur in choices regarding questions pertaining to the loss of human lives depending on framing.
The effects of frames on decision preferences are analogous to the effects of perspectives on perceptual appearance.
The dependence of preferences on the formulation of decision problems poses a significant challenge to the theory of rational choice.

limitations.text: The theory of rational choice fails to account for the dependence of preferences on the formulation of decision problems.

methodologies.name: Decision problem framing experiments
methodologies.description: Evaluating shifts and reversals in choice preferences across alternative formulations of identical decision problems.
